TPRDs not opening or venting due to fatigue of components, icing causing blockage and over-pressurization, or inadequate design and/or installation were also important scenarios explored. Also, reactive components (such as air) trapped in piping with hydrogen as well as malfunction of automatic shutoff valves were considered. A critical consideration in this analysis was the potential for a boiling liquid expanding vapor explosion (BLEVE). A BLEVE is an explosion caused by the rupture of a vessel containing a pressurized liquid above its boiling point [21]. A hydrogen BLEVE can occur if the vessel structure containing liquid hydrogen is compromised, resulting in the liquid rapidly expanding and forming a gas, possibly leading to an explosion. A hydrogen BLEVE can create a serious hazard due to the large gas release and associated detonation energy, so this scenario was an important consideration in this analysis. 1.2. Assumptions The work focused on evaluating the safety hazards of both gaseous and liquid hydrogen rail systems inside rail maintenance facilities. While pre-service defueling may occur outside in many hydrogen vehicle maintenance facilities, this work considers defueling the tank indoors, and its potential associated hazards. This study also assumes that venting is performed with a venting tool attached to the tank valve assembly which releases hydrogen up through ventilation tubing connected to the roof. Though this work may be performed by the manufacturer, disassembly and maintenance of the fuel tank as a repair was assumed to be conducted in the facility, and all such major and minor repairs/maintenance are conducted in the same facility. This analysis assumes that multiple unit cars may each hold 260 kg of hydrogen at 35 MPa or 70 MPa, while locomotives may hold 400 kg at the same pressures and a tender car may hold 135 m3 of liquid hydrogen [22]. This work considered single or paired failures only, meaning that cascading failures or instances where three or more components failed simultaneously were not analyzed. Hazards associated with 13 general, non-hydrogen-specific maintenance activities (e.g., employee ergonomic injuries and noise) were not considered since these hazards are not unique to hydrogen rail maintenance facilities. Instead, this work focused on hydrogen leaks, fire, delayed explosion, and similar consequences. Finally, refueling was also assumed to occur inside the maintenance facility. 14 2. HAZARD AND OPERABILITY ANALYSIS OF HYDROGEN RAIL IN MAINTENANCE FACILITIES This section describes the development process and the results of the hazard and operability study of hydrogen rail undergoing maintenance in an enclosed facility. This section explores unique hazards, relevant parameters involved in the analysis, and results of the analysis. 2.1. Hazard and Operability Parameters A hazard and operability study or analysis is a qualitative risk identification method which is used to identify process or equipment deviations and their resulting consequences. Relevant process parts or “nodes” are each matched with a set of common guidewords to identify a likely cause of that scenario as well as a hazardous consequence.
